Example Prompt:
Consider the relation [MATH: R] over the sets [MATH: A = \{1,2, 3,4\}] and [MATH: B = \{1,2,4,6\}] given by

[MATH: R = \big\{(1,2), (2,4), (3,1), (3,2), (4,6) \big\}.]
Explain why this relation is not functional.

Content:
EXPLANATION

Explanation:
A binary relation [MATH: R] defined over [MATH: A] and [MATH: B] is functional (or a partial function) if, for all [MATH: a \in A] and [MATH: b_1,b_2 \in B,] we have
[MATH: (a,b_1) \in R \quad\textrm{and}\quad (a,b_2) \in R
\qquad\Rightarrow\qquad
b_1 = b_2.]
In other words, if the first components of two ordered pairs are equal, then the second components must also be equal.

In this case, our relation is not functional because it contains the pairs [MATH: (3,1)] and [MATH: (3,2)] that have the same first component and different second components.

sections.normalized_html:
A binary relation [MATH: R] defined over [MATH: A] and [MATH: B] is functional (or a partial function) if, for all [MATH: a \in A] and [MATH: b_1,b_2 \in B,] we have [MATH: (a,b_1) \in R \quad\textrm{and}\quad (a,b_2) \in R \qquad\Rightarrow\qquad b_1 = b_2.] In other words, if the first components of two ordered pairs are equal, then the second components must also be equal.

In terms of digraphs, this means that no two different arrows can have the same starting node.

In this case, our relation is not functional because the digraph contains the arrows [MATH: \gamma \longrightarrow \beta \qquad\textrm{and}\qquad \gamma \longrightarrow \gamma] that have the same starting node and different ending nodes.

items.title: Identifying Functional Relations

sections.normalized_html:
Which of the following relations are functional?

  • [MATH: x \: R \: y] if and only if [MATH: x=\textrm{e}^y,] defined on [MATH: \mathbb{R}]

  • [MATH: x \: S \: y] if and only if [MATH: 2x \equiv y \:\: (\textrm{mod}\:6),] defined on [MATH: \mathbb{Z}]

  • [MATH: x \: T \: y] if and only if [MATH: x = |y|,] defined on [MATH: \mathbb{Q}]
sections.readable_text:
Which of the following relations are functional?

- [MATH: x \: R \: y] if and only if [MATH: x=\textrm{e}^y,] defined on [MATH: \mathbb{R}]
- [MATH: x \: S \: y] if and only if [MATH: 2x \equiv y \:\: (\textrm{mod}\:6),] defined on [MATH: \mathbb{Z}]
- [MATH: x \: T \: y] if and only if [MATH: x = |y|,] defined on [MATH: \mathbb{Q}]

sections.normalized_html: EXPLANATION
sections.readable_text: EXPLANATION

sections.normalized_html:
A binary relation [MATH: R] defined over [MATH: A] and [MATH: B] is functional (or a partial function) if, for all [MATH: a \in A] and [MATH: b_1,b_2 \in B,] we have [MATH: (a,b_1) \in R \quad\textrm{and}\quad (a,b_2) \in R \qquad\Rightarrow\qquad b_1 = b_2.] In other words, if the first components of two ordered pairs are equal, then the second components must also be equal.

With that in mind, let's examine our relations.

  • [MATH: R] is functional. Indeed, [MATH: a=\textrm{e}^b_1] and [MATH: a=\textrm{e}^b_2] is equivalent to [MATH: b_1 = b_2.] So, when the first components of two pairs are equal, then the second components are also equal.

  • [MATH: S] is not functional. Notice that [MATH: 2(0) \equiv 0 \: (\textrm{mod}\:6)] and also [MATH: 2(0) \equiv 6 \: (\textrm{mod}\:6).] So, [MATH: S] contains the pairs [MATH: (0,0)] and [MATH: (0,6)] with the same first component but different second components.

  • [MATH: T] is not functional. Notice that [MATH: 1 = | 1|] and [MATH: 1 = | - 1|.] So, [MATH: T] contains the pairs [MATH: (1,1)] and [MATH: (1,-1)] with the same first component but different second components.

Therefore, the correct answer is "[MATH: R] only."

items.title: Final Notes

sections.normalized_html: Let's review some of the concepts we have learned so far.
sections.readable_text: Let's review some of the concepts we have learned so far.

sections.normalized_html:
• The most general objects are sets. Everything in math is a set!

  • Next, we have relations, which are special kinds of sets, namely, sets of ordered pairs. In general, a relation can contain all kinds of ordered pairs without restrictions.

  • Then, we have functional relations (or partial functions). These are special kinds of relations that are "almost" functions. Partial functions are "deterministic" in the sense that given the first component of an ordered pair, we can uniquely determine the second component of the pair.

    In terms of mapping diagrams, we exclude situations when some input value can be assigned to more than one output value.

  • Finally, functions are functional relations where each input value is always assigned to some output value. In terms of mapping diagrams, we forbid situations where an input value is not assigned an output value.

Item 1 — Tutorial: Introduction

Content:
A binary relation [MATH: R] defined over [MATH: A] and [MATH: B] is functional (or a partial function) if, for all [MATH: a \in A] and [MATH: b_1,b_2 \in B,] we have

Content:
[MATH: (a,b_1) \in R \quad\textrm{and}\quad (a,b_2) \in R
\qquad\Rightarrow\qquad
b_1 = b_2.]

Content:
In other words, if the first components of two ordered pairs are equal, the second components must also be equal.

Content:
For example, the relation

Content:
[MATH: R = \big\{ (2,1), (3,2), (4,2) \big\},]

Content:
defined on [MATH: A = \{1,2,3,4\},] is functional. Indeed, no pairs have the same first component but distinct second components.

Content:
On the other hand, the relation

Content:
[MATH: R = \big\{ (2,1), (3,2), (4,2), (4,3) \big\},]

Content:
is not functional. Notice that it contains the pairs [MATH: ({\color{blue}4},{\color{red}2})] and [MATH: ({\color{blue}4},{\color{red}3})] that have the same first component ([MATH: {\color{blue}4}]) and different second components ([MATH: {\color{red}2}] and [MATH: {\color{red}3}]).

---

Item 2 — Example: Explaining Why a Relation Is Not Functional

Example Prompt:
Consider the relation [MATH: R] over the sets [MATH: A = \{1,2, 3,4\}] and [MATH: B = \{1,2,4,6\}] given by

[MATH: R = \big\{(1,2), (2,4), (3,1), (3,2), (4,6) \big\}.]
Explain why this relation is not functional.

Content:
EXPLANATION

Explanation:
A binary relation [MATH: R] defined over [MATH: A] and [MATH: B] is functional (or a partial function) if, for all [MATH: a \in A] and [MATH: b_1,b_2 \in B,] we have
[MATH: (a,b_1) \in R \quad\textrm{and}\quad (a,b_2) \in R
\qquad\Rightarrow\qquad
b_1 = b_2.]
In other words, if the first components of two ordered pairs are equal, then the second components must also be equal.

In this case, our relation is not functional because it contains the pairs [MATH: (3,1)] and [MATH: (3,2)] that have the same first component and different second components.

Item 5 — Tutorial: Functional Relations in Terms of Mapping Diagrams

Content:
In terms of mapping diagrams, functional relations cannot have more than one arrow starting at the same point.

Graphic:

Item 10 — Example: Identifying Functional Relations

Example Prompt:
Which of the following relations are functional?

- [MATH: x \: R \: y] if and only if [MATH: x=\textrm{e}^y,] defined on [MATH: \mathbb{R}]
- [MATH: x \: S \: y] if and only if [MATH: 2x \equiv y \:\: (\textrm{mod}\:6),] defined on [MATH: \mathbb{Z}]
- [MATH: x \: T \: y] if and only if [MATH: x = |y|,] defined on [MATH: \mathbb{Q}]

Content:
EXPLANATION

Explanation:
A binary relation [MATH: R] defined over [MATH: A] and [MATH: B] is functional (or a partial function) if, for all [MATH: a \in A] and [MATH: b_1,b_2 \in B,] we have
[MATH: (a,b_1) \in R \quad\textrm{and}\quad (a,b_2) \in R
\qquad\Rightarrow\qquad
b_1 = b_2.]
In other words, if the first components of two ordered pairs are equal, then the second components must also be equal.

With that in mind, let's examine our relations.

- [MATH: R] is functional. Indeed, [MATH: a=\textrm{e}^b_1] and [MATH: a=\textrm{e}^b_2] is equivalent to [MATH: b_1 = b_2.] So, when the first components of two pairs are equal, then the second components are also equal.
- [MATH: S] is not functional. Notice that [MATH: 2(0) \equiv 0 \: (\textrm{mod}\:6)] and also [MATH: 2(0) \equiv 6 \: (\textrm{mod}\:6).] So, [MATH: S] contains the pairs [MATH: (0,0)] and [MATH: (0,6)] with the same first component but different second components.
- [MATH: T] is not functional. Notice that [MATH: 1 = | 1|] and [MATH: 1 = | - 1|.] So, [MATH: T] contains the pairs [MATH: (1,1)] and [MATH: (1,-1)] with the same first component but different second components.

Therefore, the correct answer is "[MATH: R] only."
